items.title: Preparation composition confounds treatment effects in cochlear synaptosomal proteomics: a nested machine learning reanalysis of cisplatin and MnTBAP exposure
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Cisplatin causes permanent hearing loss in a large proportion of treated patients, and the ribbon synapse between inner hair cells and spiral ganglion neurons is an early target of this injury. Quantitative proteomics of cochlear synaptosomes can identify proteins associated with cisplatin-induced synaptic dysfunction. Because cochlear tissue is limited, these studies typically include four or fewer animals per group, which makes both machine learning performance and differential abundance vulnerable to selection bias and to differences in the tissue content of each preparation. This study tests the hypothesis that cisplatin treatment produces a cochlear synaptosomal proteome signature that is classifiable, robust to the composition of each preparation, and reversed by co-treatment with MnTBAP, a peroxynitrite scavenger. A tandem mass tag (TMT) 16-plex dataset from four groups of mice (Control, Cisplatin, MnTBAP+Cisplatin and MnTBAP, four biological replicates each) was reanalyzed from the raw reporter ion abundances using channel-level quality control, empirical Bayes moderated statistics, nested leave-one-out classification with exact permutation tests, and projection of the held-out MnTBAP groups onto the cisplatin axis. Additionally, tissue composition was quantified with six protein marker panels and an unsupervised principal component. One channel (MnTBAP+Cisplatin replicate 1) contained 10% of the median channel signal and was excluded. Of 4,667 quantified proteins, one protein differed between Cisplatin and Control at a false discovery rate (FDR) below 0.05, and 147 differed at an FDR below 0.20, a signal well above all balanced label permutations. Nested classifiers reached an area under the ROC curve of 0.75 to 0.94, and no classifier was significant by exact permutation test (p ≥ 0.086). Furthermore, the first principal component of the proteome (31.3% of variance) captured synaptic protein enrichment (r = 0.91 with a synaptic marker score) and differed between groups (p = 0.026). Cisplatin preparations were the most synapse-enriched, MnTBAP+Cisplatin preparations contained the most bone matrix and plasma protein, and MnTBAP preparations contained the most marrow and immune-cell protein. Among the 4,630 proteins with complete values, adjustment for this composition axis reduced the proportion of proteins altered by cisplatin (p 2 = 0.55), the result depended on the covariate used, and the cisplatin effect could not be separated from composition. Collectively, these findings suggest that differences in preparation composition are confounded with treatment in this dataset and may account for much of the apparent treatment effect, and that composition should be measured and modeled before synaptosomal proteomics can support treatment-specific conclusions.

items.title: Magnolia: A Persistent-Memory Agent Framework for Computational Chemistry
items.abstract_or_text: Chemistry has recently entered a high-data regime as molecular databases from high-throughput platforms or computational studies have become available. Increasing automation within the chemical sciences leads to a more digital and precision chemistry. Dedicated scientific agents are becoming central to guiding the chemist through an ever-increasing amount of data and findings, including negative ones. Here, we introduce Magnolia, a persistent-memory artificial intelligence agent framework that integrates computational protocols, from docking to quantum chemistry, lab notebooks and chat logs relying on large language models (LLMs). It relies on a three-tier memory system: session-level observations are automatically captured and distilled into structured learnings, confirmed and elevated to project-tier entries and, when human-validated, promoted to cross-project rules that actively guide subsequent work and provide direct chemical feedback. We illustrate Magnolia on four case studies: quantum-chemical evaluation of aromatic systems (COMPAS database), molecular dynamics of butane and of modified DNA, and a protein-peptide docking campaign. Across these projects, Magnolia tracked 317 runs and accumulated 116 project-tier entries, from which four cross-project rules were promoted; in controlled replays of four tasks, runs with memory passed the checks that runs without it failed (for example, ten of ten docking-configuration checks, against one to four of ten). By combining automation, reproducibility, and human-in-the-loop control, our Magnolia framework streamlines docking, molecular dynamics and quantum chemistry calculations with direct analysis and LLM-augmented feedback, offering accelerated access to computational (bio)chemistry.

items.title: LeakBench: Auditing Reward Hacking through Prediction-Time Leakage in Clinical Modeling Agents
items.abstract_or_text: Autonomous clinical-modeling agents can optimize predictive performance while violating conditions that make a model usable. We introduce LeakBench, an executable, guideline-derived audit suite that tests agent decisions for prediction-time leakage, calibration, site-level evaluation, support awareness, and decision-curve net benefit. LeakBench combines a synthetic task with known failure structure and two real-data settings: MIMIC-IV (430k admissions) and governed multi-hospital inpatient record front-page (MHFP) data. Our primary analysis uses reward hacking descriptively, without attributing intent: an agent selects prediction-time-invalid inputs because they improve its validation reward. A deterministic optimizer and every evaluated unconstrained local-model configuration select a fatal leaking feature. In fully logged September 2026 A/B runs, DeepSeek Flash and GPT-6-astra each leak in 10/10 unconstrained runs and 0/10 runs with an explicit admission-time constraint. This contrast is version-sensitive: a blinded Claude/Fable-5.1 chat run does not leak in either condition, while explicit-constraint violations appear only in a historical August 2026 slice lacking raw trajectories. Replacing AUROC with AUPRC does not remove leakage selection. Renaming or disguising the leaking inputs changes neither selection nor provenance-based detection; a name-based filter fails. A deterministic provenance verifier-in-loop removes the leak, making the LLM repair loop defense-in-depth. Specific verifier feedback clears fatal leakage in a hosted agent, and a three-seed ablation finds principle-only feedback clears decision-level defects, though these mitigation results are limited. LeakBench treats trustworthy clinical prediction as a property of an agent's modeling process, not merely its score; it is an audit testbed with known-failure controls, not yet an expert-validated benchmark.

items.title: Spatially Informed and Direction Sensitive Representation Learning for Spatial Transcriptomics
items.abstract_or_text: Cellular states are shaped by both intrinsic gene expression programs and the spatial microenvironment in which cells reside. Spatial transcriptomics makes this context measurable, but effective representation learning requires capturing both spatially informative molecular signals and intercellular organization. Existing approaches address these challenges only partially: conventional gene selection can overlook spatially structured signals, while methods for encoding cell-cell relationships often either reduce a cell's microenvironment to proximity alone, discarding direction, or rely on absolute coordinates tied to an arbitrary tissue frame. Consequently, cells with similar neighbor distances but distinct spatial organization may receive overly similar representations, despite experiencing different biological contexts that shape their cellular states. We introduce Tessera, a spatial representation learning framework that addresses both molecular selection and cellular context. Tessera combines spatially informed gene selection with a geometric inductive bias that contextualizes each cell within its local tissue environment. By modeling relative cell-cell relationships, Tessera is translation-invariant while preserving direction, allowing neighboring cells to contribute differently according to their spatial context and cellular state. Across held-out tissues and technologies, Tessera outperforms existing spatial foundation models in representation quality and generalizes zero-shot to contexts up to 16\times larger than those seen during training.

items.title: Convergent Performance, Divergent Mechanisms in LoRA-Adapted Vision Foundation Models for Brain MRI
items.abstract_or_text: Adapting Vision Foundation Models (VFMs) to medical imaging via LoRA has become standard practice, yet model selection is guided almost entirely by downstream task metrics, treating backbones with similar performance as interchangeable. We investigate whether equal performance implies equal internal representational shift. We analyse four ViT-B/16 backbones, DINOv3, SigLIP2, MerMED-FM, and BiomedCLIP, pre-trained with different objectives (self-distillation vs. contrastive vision-language) and on different data domains (natural vs. medical images). We adapt each to brain tumour segmentation and evaluate on six datasets covering both segmentation and Alzheimer's disease classification. Using attention divergence, weight-change analysis, and activation patching, we find that the four models converge to similar segmentation performance (mean Dice 78-81%) through markedly different internal dynamics, yet diverge in cross-task transfer: segmentation adaptation improves Alzheimer's disease classification for DINOv3 but degrades it for the other three backbones. We reveal a dissociation between modification magnitude and causal importance: the most heavily modified layers are not the causally relevant ones, with early-to-mid layers identified as sufficient for segmentation recovery. Restricting LoRA to these layers matches or approaches full-layer segmentation while reducing classification degradation in the three affected backbones, providing a mechanistically grounded strategy that is more parameter-efficient and more robust than standard full-layer adaptation.

items.title: Can Language Models Get "Aphasia" From Neuronal Ablation?
items.abstract_or_text: Progressive neuronal loss is the hallmark of neurodegenerative disease, yet how loss of neurons shapes the pattern of cognitive decline remains poorly understood. Here we systematically ablate neurons (computational units) in language models spanning recurrent long short-term memory (LSTM) and Transformer architectures and apply limited fine-tuning as a simple proxy for compensatory plasticity. With whole-unit ablation, LSTMs degrade gradually with syntactic and semantic faculties declining in parallel across mild-to-moderate damage. By contrast, Transformers exhibit late threshold-like collapse under feedforward multi-layer perceptron (MLP) ablation and smoother sigmoid-like decline under attention-head ablation. Qualitatively, MLP-ablated models continue to make within-category semantic substitutions (semantic paraphasias) alongside rising non-responses, paralleling Wernicke-type aphasia, while attention-head ablation produces a trend toward loss of semantic specificity similar to the semantic variant of primary progressive aphasia (svPPA). These findings indicate that feedforward and attentional pathways have functionally distinct failure modes, suggesting that architecture-dependent failure profiles may offer new computational perspectives on aphasic syndromes and neurodegenerative diseases as an in silico model. Notably, early accuracy retention under Transformer attention-head ablation qualitatively parallels pre-symptomatic reserve before the 40--60% neuronal loss reported by Gomez-Isla et al. (1996) when clinical symptoms emerge in Alzheimer's disease, whereas the steadier LSTM decline parallels the symptomatic progression described by DeKosky and Scheff (1990) and Terry et al. (1991).

items.title: Reliable and Efficient Agentic Protein Design with Toolset Harnessing
items.abstract_or_text: Computational protein design workflows require the orchestration of multiple tools, data formats, and analysis steps that are often fragmented. Here, we introduce Chaperone, a lightweight and customizable framework that enables seamless integration of RFdiffusion3 (RFD3) with downstream sequence design, structure prediction, and evaluation tools, including ProteinMPNN, AlphaFold3 (AF3), and more than 50 other protein design tools. By combining a programmable agent-friendly interface with parallelized execution on high-performance computing systems, Chaperone as a harness enables rapid iteration and scalable exploration of complex protein design workflows. Across an evaluation of nine biomolecular design tasks, we find using Chaperone reduces total token usage relative to baseline agents by 86% and GPU costs by 64%, while increasing the overall computational design pass rate. We demonstrate Chaperones utility for large-scale design-space exploration through a two-week end-to-end small-molecule binder design campaign, yielding low nanomolar binders to cortisol zero shot. We further demonstrate its versatility across distinct design challenges, including the design of a symmetric 12-subunit self-assembly nanoparticle and a linker that mediates interactions between C2- and D3-symmetric protein complexes to form crystalline assemblies. Together, these results demonstrate how agent harnesses built around standardized tool interfaces can substantially improve the efficiency and success of complex, long-horizon agentic design workflows in biology. We make Chaperone freely available to the community on GitHub: https://github.com/RosettaCommons/chaperone.

items.title: ALSmiR: a curated evidence resource for ALS-associated microRNAs for biomarker discovery
items.abstract_or_text: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is a multifactorial, late-onset neurodegenerative disease with incompletely understood pathogenesis. Limited survival after symptom onset creates an urgent need for biomarkers to support diagnosis, prognosis, and patient stratification. MicroRNAs are among the candidate biomarkers investigated in this disease. Although reviews have synthesized microRNA expression findings, differences in patient populations, biospecimens, and methods complicate comparisons. In the age of data-driven research, we need an updated, searchable resource that links each finding to its context and incorporates growing evidence. Here, we present ALSmiR, a public, manually curated database of polymerase chain reaction-based microRNA expression findings from human biological fluids and their components. ALSmiR currently contains 1,620 expression records from 49 publications comparing patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis with healthy controls, covering 816 microRNA names across 13 biospecimen categories. We link publication, cohort, and microRNA-result tables to preserve each finding's clinical and experimental context. We retain significant and non-significant results and provide searchable records and comma-separated values exports for independent analysis. We update ALSmiR annually and verify author submissions against source publications before inclusion. Researchers can use ALSmiR to assess candidate biomarkers, formulate hypotheses, and design independent validation studies. ALSmiR is freely accessible worldwide without registration at https://alsmir.dokhlab.org/.

items.title: Avoiding Data Leakage in Machine Learning Models for Diabetes and Hypertension Classification Using Routine Occupational Health Screening Data
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Background and Aim: Reliable clinical prediction using machine learning requires leakage-free model development, yet this critical methodological concern is often overlooked. Type 2 diabetes and hypertension represent major public health challenges in Iran, and early identification of at-risk individuals using routine workplace health screening data could enable cost-effective prevention. This study had a dual objective: first, to develop and validate machine learning models for identifying diabetes and hypertension using routine occupational health screening data; and second and more critically to demonstrate how the inclusion of outcome-defining predictors (fasting blood glucose and blood pressure) artificially inflates model performance through data leakage, a methodological pitfall often overlooked in clinical prediction studies. By comparing 'full' models (with all predictors) against 'clinically meaningful' models (excluding outcome-defining variables), we provide empirical evidence of the magnitude of this bias and offer a transparent framework for avoiding it in similar studies. Methods A retrospective cross-sectional analysis was conducted on 370 health screening records. Five algorithms Decision Tree, Ridge Classifier, Logistic Regression, XGBoost, and Random Forest were developed and compared. Two modeling strategies were implemented: (1) a full model including all predictors, and (2) a clinically meaningful model excluding outcome-defining predictors (fasting blood glucose and blood pressure). The dataset was split into 80% training and 20% testing sets. Five-fold cross-validation was used for hyperparameter optimization, and SMOTE was applied solely to the training set to address class imbalance. Performance was evaluated using accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, F1 score, AUC-ROC with 95% CI, calibration plots, and Brier scores. Feature importance was assessed using SHAP values. Results The prevalence of diabetes and hypertension was 18.4% (68 cases) and 20.5% (76 cases), respectively. In the clinically meaningful models that excluded outcome-defining predictors (fasting blood glucose and blood pressure), discrimination performance was moderate, with Random Forest achieving an AUC-ROC of 78.34% (95% CI: 72.15–84.92) for diabetes and 76.81% (95% CI: 70.23–83.45) for hypertension. In contrast, when these predictors were included in the full models, performance was artificially inflated (Random Forest AUC-ROC: 96.22% for diabetes and 94.59% for hypertension), confirming substantial data leakage. XGBoost performed comparably in both approaches. SHAP analysis identified age, BMI, waist circumference, and psychological distress (GSI) as the most important non-outcome predictors. Conclusion After excluding outcome-defining predictors to prevent data leakage, machine learning models particularly Random Forest and XGBoost showed moderate but clinically realistic discriminative ability for identifying diabetes and hypertension using routine screening data. Psychological variables contributed meaningfully to prediction, supporting integrated physical and mental health screening in occupational settings. External validation in independent cohorts is required before clinical implementation.

items.title: A Scalable Framework for Longitudinal Surveillance of Research Evolution in Digital Medicine
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract We developed a novel scalable framework that tracks the evolution of research topics across many journals and applied it to biomedical informatics, a field central to digital medicine, contributing methods for semantic harmonization across heterogeneous publication metadata. We analyzed 78,073 articles from 29 PubMed-indexed journals (2011–2025) carrying 95,872 distinct keywords: 75% author-supplied via PubMed or publishers, 24% substituted MeSH descriptors, 1% generated from abstracts. Three overlapping waves emerged: genomics and foundational informatics, machine learning, and generative AI. Attention shifted in 34 of 70 methodology and 22 of 86 health topics; rises persisted on author-supplied keywords alone, whereas most declines disappeared, implying that changes in keyword source, not waning attention, explain most apparent declines. Digital health technologies was the connective topic, clinical and computational collaboration grew, and the Journal of Biomedical Informatics bridged the journal communities. The framework can be applied to other biomedical research fields to identify emerging research priorities.

items.title: CODA: Cohort- and Drift-aware Foundation Model for Multimodal Clinical Reasoning
items.abstract_or_text: Recent advances in multimodal foundation models have demonstrated strong performance across diverse clinical tasks. However, existing approaches predominantly operate at the individual sample level and fail to model the interplay between population-level cohort patterns and patient-specific variation that underlie real-world clinical reasoning. In practice, clinicians routinely reason through patient cohorts sharing similar demographic, physiological, or pathological characteristics, while accounting for patient-specific deviations from the group prototype. Motivated by this gap, we propose CODA, a cohort- and drift-aware foundation model for multimodal clinical reasoning. CODA explicitly integrates cohort structure into the modeling pipeline through two complementary mechanisms: cohort-aware population stratification and drift-aware individual adaptation. In particular, we leverage reinforcement learning to discover clinically meaningful patient cohorts, and further model each patient's deviation from cohort prototypes as a structured drift signal encoding fine-grained individual heterogeneity. These cohort- and drift-aware representations are incorporated into the foundation model to enable reasoning that is simultaneously informed by population-level patterns and sensitive to individual-level variation. Extensive experiments on real-world electronic health record (EHR) benchmarks demonstrate that CODA achieves consistent effectiveness and strong generalizability across diverse clinical tasks, including closed-QA, open-QA, and report generation.

items.title: High-throughput identification of protein turnover modulators in human neurons
items.abstract_or_text: Disturbances in protein homeostasis are a defining feature of aging and neurodegenerative diseases. However, current proteomics approaches do not enable screening-scale pharmacological interrogation of protein turnover in post-mitotic human neurons. Here we establish a Mammalian Cell-optimized Fluorescent Timer (MCFT)-based live-cell imaging platform to quantify global protein synthesis and degradation rates in human embryonic stem cell-derived neurons at screening scale. Among 5,897 tested compounds, 199 increased protein synthesis and degradation rates, and three selected compounds upregulated translation-associated genes in human neurons. We then tested their ability to suppress the accumulation of pathogenic a-synuclein aggregates in models of Lewy body-like pathology. All three compounds induced efficient clearance of a-synuclein aggregates in mouse primary neurons, and one compound demonstrated similar efficacy in human dopaminergic neurons. This platform provides a broadly applicable strategy for identifying biomedically-relevant compounds that enhance protein turnover across pluripotent stem cell-derived cellular models.

items.title: Contextual Biomedical Language Models for Imbalance-Aware Drug-Food Interaction Classification
items.abstract_or_text: Drug-food interactions (DFIs) are essential to patient safety because they can alter drug effectiveness or cause side effects. Automated classification of DFIs is difficult because of unstructured textual data, semantic ambiguity, and class imbalance, especially when separating neutral interactions. This paper presents an imbalance-aware deep learning approach for classifying drug-food interactions into three classes: safe, neutral, and unsafe. A structured dataset is created from textual drug interaction descriptions by extracting drug-food pairs and labeling them using rule-based heuristics. To address class imbalance, we apply class weighting and focal loss while fine-tuning the context-aware BioBERT language model. Our experiments show that the approach reaches an accuracy of 85% and a macro-averaged F1-score of 0.77, with a notable improvement on the minority neutral class (F1-score of 0.56). The main novelty of this work is the combination of contextual biomedical language modeling with imbalance-aware deep learning, enabling more effective classification of DFI datasets.

items.title: Pharmacologic inhibition of OLIG2 by CT-179 disrupts mitotic progression and enhances standard-of-care chemoradiotherapy in glioblastoma
items.abstract_or_text: Background: Glioblastoma (GBM) remains uniformly fatal. The basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor OLIG2 is universally expressed in diffuse glioma, sustains the tumor-propagating stem-like fraction, and opposes p53-mediated genotoxic responses, but has historically been considered undruggable. We characterized CT-179, a brain-penetrant small-molecule OLIG2 inhibitor, as a candidate therapeutic for GBM. Methods: Target engagement was assessed by cellular thermal shift assay, differential scanning fluorimetry, crosslinking, and electrophoretic mobility shift assay. Anti-tumor activity was evaluated across eleven patient-derived GBM cell lines, in zebrafish oligodendrocyte precursor cell (OPC)-derived tumors, and orthotopic and subcutaneous GBM models, including combinations with radiotherapy plus temozolomide and with selective Bcl-2 family inhibitors. Results: CT-179 engaged OLIG2 and altered the conformation of dimerized OLIG2 on chromatin without preventing dimerization or fully displacing OLIG2 from DNA. CT-179 reduced OLIG2-positive OPCs and OPC-derived tumors in zebrafish and inhibited proliferation across all eleven GBM lines (IC50 < 360 nM), depleting the stem-like fraction and inducing apoptosis through mitotic catastrophe, mitotic slippage, or a hybrid response. RNA-seq across three patient-derived glioma stem cell lines identified {beta}-tubulin gene isoforms as the most strongly CT-179-down-regulated transcripts at the early time point and showed correlated {beta}-tubulin and OLIG2 expression in TCGA glioblastoma specimens. Combination with the Mcl-1 inhibitor S63845 or the Bcl-2/Bcl-xL/Bcl-w inhibitor ABT-737 produced greater-than-additive cytotoxicity. Oral CT-179 crossed the blood-brain barrier and extended median survival as a single agent across two independent adult orthotopic patient-derived backgrounds (GBM8 and G06); intraperitoneal CT-179 was associated with reduced intratumoral OLIG2 and Ki-67 staining in GBM8 orthotopic xenografts. Combination of CT-179 with radiotherapy and temozolomide eliminated all GBM8 and 7 of 8 GBM4 subcutaneous xenografts without weight loss and significantly extended survival when combined with radiotherapy in MGMT-unmethylated GBM6 orthotopic xenografts (CT-179 administered intraperitoneally). Conclusions: CT-179 is a brain-penetrant inhibitor of an established GBM driver with single-agent and combination activity across several orthotopic models, supporting clinical development for GBM and translational evaluation in other OLIG2-dependent CNS malignancies.

items.title: Convergent and Divergent Neural Signatures of Cue-Induced Response in Substance and Behavioral Addictions: A Coordinate-Based Neuroimaging Meta-Analysis
items.abstract_or_text: Addiction-related cues trigger craving and precipitate relapse, yet whether substance use disorders (SUDs) and behavioral addictions (BAs) share a universal neurobiological cue-reactivity core remains unresolved. We conducted a coordinate-based meta-analysis using Seed-based d Mapping with Permutation of Subject Images (SDM-PSI) to synthesize whole-brain fMRI studies comparing visually evoked cue-reactivity in strictly diagnosed SUDs and BAs versus healthy controls. An updated systematic search through September 12, 2026, yielded 50 eligible articles comprising 53 independent contrasts and 2,578 participants. Pooled analyses across all addictions revealed convergent cue-elicited activations in the mid-cingulate cortex, precentral gyrus, and a midline midbrain region. However, a formal SUD {cap} BA conjunction analysis yielded no family-wise error (FWE)-corrected shared clusters. Direct comparisons demonstrated greater activation in the left hippocampus, pregenual anterior cingulate cortex, and precuneus for SUDs relative to BAs. Importantly, the left hippocampal and precuneus differences survived age adjustment; furthermore, the hippocampal finding remained robust when restricting analyses to highly controlled cue-versus-neutral paradigms, while the precuneus finding was retained within picture-cue modalities. Furthermore, exploratory analyses of clinical characteristics indicated that cue-elicited neural responses were associated with specific clinical states and treatment variables (e.g., methadone maintenance in heroin use disorder), highlighting the modulatory effect of clinical symptom profiles on these regional functional signatures. Overall, the results motivate further investigation of memory- and self-related processes, as well as control- or action-related processes. These findings offer a critical foundation for developing targeted clinical interventions, distinguishing between generalized transdiagnostic neuromodulation targets and disorder-specific therapies tailored to distinct clinical and demographic profile.

items.title: From Supportive Care to Precision Medicine: Emerging Therapies for Inherited Epidermolysis Bullosa
items.abstract_or_text: Background: Inherited epidermolysis bullosa (EB) comprises monogenic disorders characterised by tissue fragility, recurrent blistering, chronic wounds and multisystem complications. Although multidisciplinary supportive care remains fundamental, it cannot correct the molecular defect or prevent cumulative tissue damage. This narrative review examines emerging disease-modifying therapies for inherited EB, emphasising their application in clinical practice. Methods: Pub-Med/MEDLINE was searched using terms relating to EB subtypes and pharmacological, gene-, RNA-, protein-, cell- and genome-editing therapies. Reference lists, clinical guidelines, consensus statements and regulatory documents were also examined. Clinical studies and preclinical investi-gations were synthesised qualitatively; no meta-analysis was performed. Results: Recent advances have expanded treatment beyond conventional wound care. Oleogel-S10 enhances endogenous wound healing independently of genotype, whereas beremagene geperpavec delivers functional COL7A1 copies directly to dystrophic EB wounds. Prademagene zamikeracel combines ex vivo correction of autologous keratinocytes with epidermal grafting, offering potentially sustained clo-sure of selected chronic wounds. Nevertheless, these treatments remain predominantly local and do not fully address generalised skin fragility or extracutaneous disease. Mesenchymal stromal cells, haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, recombinant type VII collagen, RNA-based treatments and genome editing may provide broader or more durable benefits, but evidence remains limited and concerns regarding delivery, safety, durability and accessibility persist. Conclusion: Precision and regenerative therapies are transforming EB management but remain complementary to multi-disciplinary supportive care. Clinical evaluation should extend beyond wound closure to include pain, function, growth, quality of life and caregiver burden. Long-term surveillance and personal-ised combination strategies are essential to determine whether early treatment can safely alter the natural history of EB.

items.title: Cross-Omics Identification of Core Epithelial Genes Associated with Folate Metabolism in Cervical Cancer and Prediction of an IL1RN/VEGFA Diagnostic Model and Candidate Drugs
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract This study integrated single-cell transcriptomics, bulk transcriptomics, GWAS, spatial transcriptomics, and drug-gene data to identify core epithelial genes associated with folate metabolism in cervical cancer. scPagwas revealed the strongest association between epithelial cells and genetic risk for the disease; hdWGCNA and WGCNA, combined with differential expression and folate metabolism gene sets, identified IL1RN and VEGFA. In the CESC cohort, IL1RN expression was downregulated and VEGFA was upregulated; external validation confirmed this trend, and the AUC of the two-gene diagnostic model was 0.771 (95% CI: 0.685–0.848). Enrichment analysis indicated that both genes are involved in DNA repair, the cell cycle, the VEGF/mTOR pathway, and the folate one-carbon pathway, and are associated with immune infiltration. Single-cell localization analysis showed that both IL1RN and VEGFA are expressed in epithelial cells; pseudo-time-series, virtual knockout, and spatial transcriptomics analyses revealed their dynamic expression, regulatory networks, and spatial heterogeneity. Molecular docking analysis demonstrated that beclomethasone can simultaneously target both IL1RN and VEGFA. In summary, IL1RN/VEGFA may serve as potential diagnostic biomarkers for cervical cancer, and beclomethasone is a candidate therapeutic agent.

items.title: Comparative Evaluation of Machine Learning Models for Heart Disease Prediction: Performance, Calibration, Threshold Selection, and Explainability
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Cardiovascular disease remains the leading global cause of death, yet machine-learning studies report widely differing results on small benchmark datasets. This study compared five supervised classifiers using the processed Cleveland Heart Disease dataset, which contains 303 records: 139 with angiographic heart disease and 164 without disease. A stratified 70/30 split allocated 212 records to training and 91 to testing. Imputation, scaling, and categorical encoding were fitted only to training data. Logistic regression achieved the best overall test performance, with 85.71% accuracy, 85.37% precision, 83.33% sensitivity, 87.76% specificity, an F1 score of 84.34%, an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC) of 0.939, and a Brier score of 0.102. Raising the classification threshold from 0.50 to a training-derived value of 0.552 increased specificity to 89.80% but reduced sensitivity to 80.95% and did not improve accuracy. Permutation importance ranked the number of major vessels, chest-pain type, and thallium test result as the leading predictors. Cross-validation F1 increased as the training sample grew. These results support multi-metric evaluation but require external validation before generalization to populations not represented in the development data, including those in sub-Saharan Africa.

items.title: An Interferon-Responsive Cancer-Associated Fibroblast Subtype Shapes an Immune-Active Tumor Microenvironment and Favors Survival in Ovarian Cancer
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Background Accumulating studies have demonstrated that discrete subsets of cancer-associated fibroblast (CAF) can potentiate antitumor immunity and are associated with favorable clinical outcomes across multiple malignancies. However, the role of CAFs within the ovarian cancer immune microenvironment remains poorly understood, and their prognostic relevance has not been fully elucidated. Methods Comprehensive transcriptomic analyses were conducted using datasets from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) to identify a prognosis-favorable subtype of CAF in high grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSOC). Single-cell and spatial transcriptomic analyses revealed intimate crosstalk between this CAF subtype and intratumoral immune cells, with these fibroblasts preferentially aggregated in tumor immune-infiltrated parenchyma. Furthermore, in vitro transcriptomic and proteomic profiling validated that type I interferon drives the differentiation of this subtype. Finally, an optimal prognostic model was established using 117 machine learning algorithms based on subtype-specific marker genes. Results An interferon-hyperresponsive CAF subpopulation was identified, named MP4-high-CAF in HGSOC, which recruits immune cells and predicts superior overall survival. Besides, a prognostic signature based on MP4-high-CAF marker genes that reliably predicts clinical outcomes in HGSOC patients was constructed and validated using a combinatorial machine-learning strategy. Conclusion This study established MP4-high-CAF as a central orchestrator of immune remodeling and a positive prognosis biomarker in HGSOC. The identified eight-genes derived from MP4-high-CAF signature exhibited promising translational value for risk stratification in HGSOC, pending additional clinical validation. Exogenous interferon stimulation may be beneficial for improving the immune microenvironment of ovarian cancer.

items.title: MoveBench: A Rubric-Based Benchmark for Evaluating Large Language Models in Sports and Health Coaching
items.abstract_or_text: Despite rapid advances in large language models (LLMs), their deployment in the sports and health domain remains high-risk due to the absence of domain-specific evaluation benchmarks. Existing general-purpose benchmarks (e.g., MMLU and HELM) primarily assess broad knowledge and reasoning capabilities, but fail to capture critical domain requirements such as exercise safety, physiological appropriateness, personalization, and actionable coaching quality. This gap is particularly concerning in fitness and health applications, where incorrect or unsafe recommendations can lead to physical harm. To address this limitation, we introduce MoveBench, the first comprehensive benchmarking framework specifically designed for evaluating LLMs in sports and health coaching. The proposed benchmark integrates heterogeneous task formats, including multiple-choice questions (MCQs) and open-ended question answering (OpenQA), grounded in real-world user scenarios and paired with structured rubrics emphasizing safety compliance, scientific validity, and training logic. Through large-scale evaluation of 15 diverse LLMs on 809 questions with 5,012 rubric-level criteria, our results reveal substantial performance variability, particularly in safety awareness, structured program design, and personalization capability, highlighting a critical gap between knowing and doing. Our work establishes a foundational evaluation standard for sports and health LLM applications and provides a reproducible framework for advancing safe, reliable, and context-aware AI-driven coaching systems. Open resources are available at https://github.com/SatoSakula/MoveBench.

items.title: PFedQFT: Personalized Federated Quantum-Inspired Fine-Tuning for Medical Large Language Models
items.abstract_or_text: Medical data remain fragmented across institutional silos because of privacy, governance, and ownership constraints. Federated learning enables medical institutions to adapt large language models (LLMs) collaboratively without transferring raw records. However, independently parameterized low-rank adapters incur repeated parameter and communication costs across Transformer projections, while uniform aggregation may limit adaptation to heterogeneous institutional data. We propose PFedQFT, a quantum-inspired framework for personalized federated fine-tuning with a compact shared adapter. Specifically, PFedQFT constructs reusable orthonormal adaptation bases from compact skew-symmetric generators using a truncated matrix-exponential approximation followed by QR orthonormalization. Compatible projections reuse these bases, while a globally shared full core preserves the flexibility of each projection. Each client further maintains a lightweight private residual operator, whose directions are learned globally and whose coefficients remain local. Experiments on seven public medical tasks and multiple LLM backbones show substantial reductions in trainable parameters and per-round adapter upload volume, with competitive predictive performance on most tasks.

items.title: Determinants of cysteine coverage by chemoproteomics
items.abstract_or_text: Covalent chemoproteomics has become a powerful route to expanding the druggable proteome, enabling proteome-wide screening of compounds that covalently modify nucleophilic residues, most commonly cysteine. Yet typical experiments detect only 5-18% of the ~250,000 cysteines encoded by the human proteome, and the determinants of this limited coverage remain poorlydefined. Here we combine cysteine featurisation, explainable machine learning (ML) and robust statistical filtering to establish what governs cysteine detectability in iodoacetamide- desthiobiotin (IA-DTB) chemoproteomics. Using a scalable feature-generation pipeline, we computed physicochemical and structural properties for cysteines and the corresponding tryptic peptides and trained models that predict detectability with high accuracy. Shapley analysis identifies protein abundance and intrinsic peptide properties governing LC-MS behaviour as the dominant determinants, whereas cysteine structural descriptors contribute comparatively little, indicating that detection is constrained downstream of probe reactivity. We further introduce a distance-based statistical filter that improves reproducibility across replicates, and show that cell line selection, subcellular fractionation and alternative electrophiles together expand coverage by >30%. More broadly, this work moves optimisation of chemoproteomics workflows from empirical trial-and-error towards rational, data-driven design.

items.title: Learning Protein-Protein Interaction Interfaces from Multimodal Representations
items.abstract_or_text: Background: Protein-protein interactions govern essential cellular processes, making the identification of interface residues critical for protein engineering and molecular design. Although complex deep learning algorithms like AlphaFold3 generate full atom resolution assemblies, they are not optimized for residue-level interface identification. Existing methods face inherent limitations: sequence-based models lack explicit 3D context, while structure-based approaches can overlook evolutionary signals. Results: By combining evolutionary context with 3D geometry, the multimodal protein language model ESM3 offers the ideal foundation for residue-level interface classification. This results in the ESM3-PPISites model, which outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods across diverse training and benchmark sets. Generalization is assessed through stringent sequence- and structure-based redundancy filtering to ensure evaluation on previously unseen proteins. Notably, finetuning the open-weight ESM3 architecture meaningfully narrows the performance gap with its proprietary full-scale counterpart. Furthermore, integrating predicted interaction sites as spatial restraints into HADDOCK significantly improves the recovery of near-native binding poses while reducing computational search time by an order of magnitude compared with blind docking. Conclusions: ESM3-PPISites enables accurate interfaces identification without relying on complex structural inputs at inference time, establishing a reliable and computationally efficient strategy for mapping protein-protein interaction sites.

items.title: GEO-BERT: A Retrieval augmented LLM Framework for Intelligent Dataset Retrieval from the Gene Expression Omnibus
items.abstract_or_text: The Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) is a commonly used data repository of high throughput gene expression and other functional genomics data. This platform is globally used by researchers for submitting experimental datasets, accessing these datasets for hypothesis validation, reusing them in data-driven research, generating ideas for new research directions. Despite global usage, searching and identifying relevant and usable datasets in GEO remains challenging with an underlying keyword based search system needing manual intervention for the retrieval of desired datasets. GEO's inconsistent metadata and varying data annotation practices across submissions, variable data quality are contributing to its challenge for building structured query tools. With the recent advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs), it is timely to revisit the GEO datasets and its query system. Here, we present an AI chat-bot, GEO-BERT, leveraging an underlying retrieval augmented generator framework on the GEO metadata with a novel hierarchical hybrid field aware retrieval system to mine the datasets. GEO-BERT is locally installable, available for programmers and project developers (https://github.com/mrumi/GEOBERTtest) and readily usable by regular users on subset of test data. We demonstrated that GEO-BERT enhances the semantic search performance not currently available by any of the leading existing AI-powered chatbots, while improving the performance of GEO's traditional search performance for project development. Given the global usage of GEO and the latest advancement of the large language models, GEO-BERT fills the gap for context-aware extraction of GEO datasets.

items.title: Going beyond labels: Semi-supervised learning for enzyme kinetic parameter prediction
items.abstract_or_text: Enzyme kinetic parameters, such as the turnover number (kcat), underpin enzyme engineering and metabolic modeling. Machine learning models can predict these parameters from sequence and substrate representations, but their accuracy is limited by the scarcity and narrow coverage of experimentally labeled data, particularly for out-of-distribution enzymes. Existing strategies to exploit unlabeled data rely on homologous sequences, pseudo-labels or synthetic perturbations of labeled samples, limiting their potential to fully leverage unlabeled data for model improvement. Here, we show that regularization-based semi-supervised learning improves model performance by leveraging biologically meaningful unlabeled samples alongside labeled data during task-specific training, without assigning pseudo-labels to the unlabeled samples. Specifically, enzyme-substrate pairs lacking kcat, but characterized for other kinetic parameters, can serve as unlabeled data that improve kcat prediction. Using the clustered CataPro dataset at 40% sequence identity as a stringent benchmark, neural consistency regularization and graph-Laplacian regularization each performed better when unlabeled records were added, beyond the gains from regularization on labeled data alone. The benefit required sufficient labeled data, saturated at a few thousand unlabeled records for the neural model, and depended on the density of the unlabeled data in the feature space rather than on their proximity to labeled data. Gains extended to wild-type and mutant enzymes and to a local low-data adenylate kinase landscape. These findings show that incomplete kinetic records specifically, and unlabeled data points generally, are a valuable resource for enzyme kinetics prediction.

items.title: Sphingosine-1-Phosphate Restrains Foamy Macrophage Formation and Modulates Inflammation in Multidrug-Resistant Tuberculosis
items.abstract_or_text: The high abundance of lipid loaded foamy macrophages in the granulomatous lesions is a key hallmark of advanced pulmonary tuberculosis. These macrophages serve as lipid-rich intracellular hiding niches that provides Mycobacterium tuberculosis (M.tb) survival and persistence during prolonged anti-tubercular treatment. Persistent infection and dysregulated inflammatory responses further complicate disease control, particularly in multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB), highlighting the need for host-directed therapeutic strategies. Our previous preclinical study demonstrated the therapeutic potential of the host sphingolipid sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) in reducing the mycobacterial burden in M.tb-infected animals, accompanied by enhanced pulmonary macrophage activation. To explore its translational potential, we investigated whether S1P modulates foamy macrophage formation in CD14 monocyte-derived macrophages from healthy donors and patients with MDR-TB. Notably, macrophages derived from patients with MDR-TB exhibited greater intracellular lipid droplet accumulation than those derived from healthy donors. This phenotype was further characterized by increased nitric oxide production and quantitative RT-PCR analysis of genes associated with immune regulation and lipid metabolism, including APOE, LDLR1, CLEC4E, CLEC7A, GP96, IL4, and IL13, which suggested a Th2-associated immunological bias in foamy macrophages. Collectively, these findings highlight the potential role of host sphingolipids in modulating foamy macrophage phenotypes and associated immunometabolic dysregulation, supporting further investigation of S1P as a host-directed therapeutic strategy against MDR-TB.

items.title: Beyond AUROC: External Validation, Calibration, and Explainability of Machine Learning Models for 30-Day Hospital Readmission Using Electronic Health Records—A Rapid Systematic Review
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Studies evaluating machine learning (ML) algorithms predicting 30-day hospital readmission using EHRs have relied on AUROC as a sole criterion. The AUROC score provides no insight into whether an ML model transfers to new hospitals or periods, whether the probabilities provided are calibrated, or whether the explanation offered can be trusted. This study was conducted as a rapid systematic review using streamlined methods informed by Cochrane rapid review guidance and reported according to the applicable PRISMA 2020 reporting items. It examined the extent to which EHR-based machine learning studies predicting 30-day hospital readmission reported external or temporal validation, calibration, explainability, clinical utility, and subgroup fairness. PubMed and Europe PMC databases were searched for studies conducted between January 2020 and October 2026, resulting in the screening of 1,644 records in two phases and inclusion of 156 studies coded based on their abstracts. Out of 62 studies providing an AUROC score for readmission as the only outcome, the median highest AUROC score was 0.76 (interquartile range 0.69--0.85).
